title: A Town of Palaces
tagline: A Jesuit who taught the memory palace in China, and how to link many palaces into a network that holds a whole subject.
card: How to go beyond one building: several palaces, bridges between them, and a plan so that nothing gets mixed up.
goal: you will learn why one palace is not enough, link palaces with vivid bridges, plan a network with a hub, and keep each building distinct.

left_off.q: How many digits does a three-digit picture hold?
left_off.a: Three: a consonant, a vowel and a consonant.

left_off.q: Why is the three-digit system more costly to learn than PAO?
left_off.a: It needs a thousand pictures, against PAO's three lists of a hundred.

left_off.q: What do you do when a syllable is not a word?
left_off.a: Use a sound-alike, a name or an abbreviation, and always the same one.

text: China, the late sixteenth century. An Italian priest of the Jesuit order, Matteo Ricci, has lived in the country for years. He has learned to speak, read and write Chinese, and dresses as a scholar. He is there to talk about his religion, but he has found that the best door into Chinese society is a surprising one: his memory.

In China, ambitious young men prepared for years for the imperial examinations, which tested their knowledge of an enormous body of classical texts. Memory was a serious matter. When Ricci reportedly showed scholars that he could learn a long list of Chinese characters, read once, and say it back in order, and then backwards, they wanted to know how.

check.q: Why were people in China interested in Ricci's memory?
check.a: Exam candidates needed to memorise a huge number of texts, so a method that worked on long lists of characters was valuable.

parts.talk: What is the largest body of material you have ever had to memorise for an exam?

text: In 1596 he wrote a short book in Chinese to explain the art. In it he taught the memory palace. He told his readers to choose a building, to fix places in it, and to put a picture in each place. He explained that the scholar should fix places in order and walk through them. He did not present it as his own invention; it came from the West.

The scholars who read it faced the same problem as every student with a lot to learn. A single building is not enough. One house with fifty places holds fifty things, and the examination was thousands of lines long. What they needed was more buildings, and a way to move between them.

check.q: What did Ricci teach in his book?
check.a: The memory palace: choosing a building, fixing places in it and putting a picture in each.

parts.talk: How many places do you think you could find in the buildings you know well?

text: Which is exactly where this lesson begins. A network of palaces is like a town. You do not memorise one house; you memorise streets, and the streets connect houses, and each house is about one subject. A bank of buildings for history, another for languages, another for your job.

The part of the network that matters most is not the houses but the connections. A good connection is a short, vivid step between the last place of one palace and the first of the next. With those, a hundred buildings can be walked in one long journey, and you can enter and leave wherever you want.

check.q: What is the most important part of a network?
check.a: The connections between palaces: a short, vivid link from the last place of one to the first of the next.

parts.talk: Which five places that you know well could be the start of a network?

source: Matteo Ricci (1552 to 1610) wrote a treatise on the art of memory in Chinese in 1596. Retold here in our own words.

method.x: One palace holds as many items as it has places. A network of palaces holds a subject, a course, or a career.

data.label: A network of palaces: a hub and three subject palaces

method.cap: A hub connected to three subject palaces, with a bridge between two of them.

items.x: History in your old school, languages in your grandmother's house, work in your office.
Different styles, colours, sizes: so you never mix a room of one with a room of another.
A place you know very well, with doors to the others. Your own home works.
A vivid, short link, for example: you open the front door of your home and walk straight into the school playground.
A list of palaces, what is in each, and how many places are free.

method.title: A bridge
method.given: From the last place of the history palace (the school hall) to the first place of the languages palace (your grandmother's front door).
lines: The school hall: a giant clock on the stage.
The clock's pendulum swings out of the door, and when it comes back it is a door knocker shaped like a parrot.
Your grandmother's front door: the parrot knocker greets you in five languages.
method.pic: The clock's pendulum swings out of the school hall and comes back as a parrot-shaped door knocker on grandmother's front door.

items: Fifty places per palace is a lot. Twenty to thirty is a good size to start with.
Keep one palace per subject. A subject that overflows gets a second building and a bridge.
Keep the order fixed in each, and the order of buildings fixed along the journey.
Reuse after clearing. When a palace is no longer needed, clear it by imagining it empty, clean and bright.
Review the bridges. The weak point of a network is a connection that has faded.

try.title: Plan a small network
try.prompt: Choose three subjects you want to keep. For each, name a building you know well, and say how it differs from the others. Add a hub.
try.model: Hub: my flat. History: my old school (a red brick building, long corridors). Languages: my grandmother's house (small, warm, full of plants). Work: the office (glass and steel). All three look very different from each other.
checks: There are three palaces and a hub.
Each is a place I know well.
They look different from each other.

try.title: A bridge
try.prompt: Write a bridge from the last place of your first palace to the first place of your second palace. Make it vivid and short.
try.model: The last place of the school is the front gate. A banner from the gate flies across the street and wraps itself round the front door of my grandmother's house like a ribbon.
checks: It starts at the last place of the first palace.
It ends at the first place of the second.

try.title: Which size?
try.prompt: Match each task to the size of palace network.
pairs: A subject you want to keep for years

try.q: A friend uses the same house for history and languages and keeps mixing them up. What do you advise?
opts: Use a different, distinct building for each subject
try.why: Distinct buildings stop one subject leaking into another.

try.title: Walk the network
try.prompt: Walk through your hub and your three palaces in order aloud, naming the first and last place of each and the bridges.

quiz.q: Why use more than one palace?
opts: One palace holds only as many items as it has places

quiz.q: What is the weak point of a network?
quiz.why: If a bridge fades, you may not get across.

quiz.q: How many places is a good size for a palace to start with?
quiz.why: Big enough to hold something, small enough to keep distinct.

quiz.q: What should you do with a palace you no longer need?
opts: Clear it by imagining it empty and clean

challenge.title: Memory challenge: the eight planets across two palaces
challenge.intro: Put the first four planets in palace A and the next four in palace B, with a bridge between. Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars | Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Type them in order.
challenge.study: Four in the first palace; a bridge; four in the second palace.

look_back.q: What does the middle digit give in the three-digit system?
In the timeline palace, what is a room?
How do you get faster at memorising?
look_back.a: Find the slowest step and make it automatic.

look_back.q: What is the method of loci?
look_back.a: Using places along a fixed route to store pictures in order.
